titulo: Hands off the thermostat: why central bank independence is worth defending

fuente.nota: Written for the language panel. The figures are approximate and should not be cited as a source.

parrafos: Every few years, a politician rediscovers an old grievance: that interest rates are set by unelected officials who answer to no one. The complaint is resurfacing on both sides of the Atlantic, as governments burdened by heavy debts and impatient voters look enviously at the levers controlled by their central banks. Some propose giving finance ministries a say in setting rates; others merely want the freedom to criticise more loudly. It is a temptation that should be resisted, though not for the reasons usually given.

The case for independence is, at heart, a case about time. Politicians face elections every four or five years, and the benefits of cheap money arrive quickly: lower mortgage payments, buoyant asset prices, a burst of hiring. The costs, in the form of higher inflation, tend to show up later, often after the votes have been counted. A government that controls monetary policy will always be tempted to borrow prosperity from the future. Knowing this, workers, firms and investors anticipate higher inflation and demand higher wages and interest rates, so the economy ends up with more inflation and no extra growth.

This insight, formalised by economists in the late 1970s and early 1980s, inspired a wave of reforms. From New Zealand to the United Kingdom, and above all in the design of the European Central Bank, legislators handed control of interest rates to institutions with a clear mandate and protection from day-to-day political interference. The ECB enjoys one of the strongest forms of independence in the world, enshrined in a treaty that can only be amended by unanimity. The results were broadly encouraging: inflation in most advanced economies fell and, for a quarter of a century, stayed close to target.

Yet independence has never been a law of nature, and its critics are not merely populists in search of a scapegoat. Since the financial crisis of 2008, central banks have accumulated powers that go far beyond adjusting a single interest rate. They have bought government and corporate bonds on a vast scale, supervised banks, rescued markets in distress and, in some cases, taken positions on climate change or inequality. Their balance sheets swelled to sums equivalent to a third or more of national output. Decisions with such large distributional consequences inevitably invite the question: who gave them the right?

The inflation surge of 2021–23 added a further charge to the indictment. Most central banks were slow to react, initially describing the rise in prices as transitory. When they finally moved, they raised rates at the fastest pace in decades, pushing up mortgage costs and the interest bill of heavily indebted governments. For critics, the episode proved that technocrats are no more infallible than elected ministers. For a finance minister staring at a soaring debt-service bill, it also provided a convenient target. Some even argued that higher rates did more to raise housing costs for young families than to tame prices driven by energy shocks beyond any central bank’s control.

Herein lies the danger. Pressure on central banks rarely takes the form of an outright abolition of their independence. It is subtler: public attacks on their leadership, appointments chosen for loyalty rather than competence, threats to revise their mandate or audit their decisions, hints that their profits should be redirected to the treasury. Each step, taken alone, may appear defensible. Together, they erode a credibility that took decades to build, and markets are quick to notice. A rise in long-term interest rates is often the first symptom of a central bank perceived as captured.

History offers sobering examples. Countries where governments have forced central banks to keep rates low in the face of rising prices have frequently ended up with runaway inflation, collapsing currencies and, eventually, interest rates far higher than those they had tried to avoid. Even in advanced economies, periods of close political control in the post-war decades coincided with bouts of inflation that proved painful to eradicate. The cost falls disproportionately on the poorest, who have no means of protecting their savings. Independence, in this sense, is not a privilege granted to bankers but a form of insurance for citizens.

None of this means that central banks should be beyond scrutiny. Independence is defensible only if it comes with accountability. That requires a narrow, clearly defined mandate set by elected representatives; regular appearances before parliament; transparent communication about decisions and the reasoning behind them; and an honest acknowledgement of mistakes. Some institutions have already published frank reviews of their recent forecasting errors; others have been far more reluctant. Central banks have also been unwise to stray into areas where their democratic legitimacy is thin. The more tasks they take on, the more they expose themselves to the accusation of governing without a mandate.

There is also a case for clarifying the boundary between monetary and fiscal policy. When a central bank holds a large share of public debt, its decisions on interest rates directly affect the budget. That interdependence is unavoidable, but it should be managed through clear rules on bond purchases and on how losses or profits are shared with the treasury, rather than through informal pressure behind closed doors. Clear arrangements would also make it harder for any government to claim that the central bank is either secretly financing or deliberately undermining its budget.

The paradox of independence is that it depends on politics. A law can protect a central bank from interference, but laws can be changed and treaties reinterpreted. What ultimately sustains independence is a broad consensus that price stability is a public good worth shielding from short-term calculation. That consensus is fragile and must be renewed by each generation. Central bankers can help by staying within their remit and explaining themselves better. Politicians, for their part, should remember that the thermostat is out of their reach for a reason: those who turn up the heat before an election rarely pay the bill.
titulo_es: Hands off the thermostat: why central bank independence is worth defending
resumen_es: An opinion piece that defends the independence of central banks against political pressure, acknowledging the criticisms and calling in return for greater accountability and a narrowly defined mandate.

ideas_clave.idea: Political complaints about unelected central bankers are returning as indebted governments covet control over interest rates, and the author argues this should be resisted.
Independence is justified by time horizons: governments gain quickly from cheap money while inflation comes later, and anticipating this, agents push up wages and rates without any gain in growth.
This reasoning led to reforms giving central banks, notably the ECB, legal protection and clear mandates, after which inflation remained low for decades.
Critics have valid points: since 2008 central banks have gained vast powers with distributional effects, and their slow response to the 2021–23 inflation showed they can err.
The real threat is gradual erosion through attacks, loyal appointments and mandate changes, which damages credibility and pushes up long-term rates.
Historical experience shows that politically controlled monetary policy ends in high inflation that hurts the poor most, so independence protects citizens.
Independence must be paired with accountability, a narrow mandate and clear rules separating monetary and fiscal policy.
Ultimately independence rests on a political consensus that must be renewed, with both central bankers and politicians showing restraint.

resumen_modelo: The author defends central bank independence at a time when governments with heavy debts are increasingly tempted to challenge it. The main argument concerns time horizons: politicians reap the benefits of cheap money before elections, while the inflationary costs emerge later; since the public anticipates this bias, the result is merely higher inflation without additional growth. This reasoning underpinned reforms that granted institutions such as the ECB strong legal protection, followed by decades of low inflation. Nonetheless, the writer concedes that criticism is not baseless. Since 2008, central banks have acquired far-reaching powers with significant distributional effects, and their belated reaction to the recent inflation surge proved they are fallible. The greatest risk, however, lies not in outright abolition but in a gradual erosion of autonomy through public attacks, politically motivated appointments or changes to mandates, which undermines credibility and raises long-term interest rates. History suggests that subordinating monetary policy to governments leads to high inflation, which hits the poorest hardest. Consequently, the author presents independence as a safeguard for citizens, provided it is matched by accountability: a narrow mandate, transparency before parliament and clear rules governing relations with the treasury. Finally, the article stresses that independence ultimately depends on a fragile political consensus that requires restraint from both central bankers and politicians.

preguntas.pregunta: What is the author’s position on the renewed political criticism of central banks?
opciones: It is entirely justified and should lead to reform
The temptation should be resisted, though not for the usual reasons
It only exists in the United States
It is irrelevant because central banks cannot be reformed
respuestas: The temptation should be resisted, though not for the usual reasons
preguntas.cita: It is a temptation that should be resisted, though not for the reasons usually given.
preguntas.explicacion: The author states from the outset that this temptation must be resisted, although with arguments different from the usual ones. The criticism arises “on both sides of the Atlantic”, not only in the US.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: According to the text, the costs of cheap money usually appear before an election.
preguntas.cita: The costs, in the form of higher inflation, tend to show up later, often after the votes have been counted.
preguntas.explicacion: It is the benefits that come quickly; the costs (higher inflation) appear later, often after the elections. The terms have been reversed.

preguntas.enunciado: Answer in your own words (1–3 sentences).
preguntas.pregunta: Why does political control of monetary policy lead to ‘more inflation and no extra growth’?
respuestas: Because people know that governments are tempted to use cheap money for short-term gains, so they expect higher inflation and ask for higher wages and interest rates in advance. These expectations cancel out any boost to growth and only leave higher inflation.
preguntas.cita: Knowing this, workers, firms and investors anticipate higher inflation and demand higher wages and interest rates
preguntas.explicacion: This is the time-inconsistency argument (KYDLAND-PRESCOTT, BARRO-GORDON): rational expectations cancel out the real effect of expansionary policy and only the inflation bias remains.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: The legal basis of the ECB’s independence can be changed only if all signatories agree.
preguntas.cita: enshrined in a treaty that can only be amended by unanimity
preguntas.explicacion: The text says that the ECB's independence is laid down in a treaty that can only be changed unanimously, that is, with everyone's agreement.

preguntas.enunciado: Find a word in paragraph 3 that means “a person or group unfairly blamed for problems”.
preguntas.pregunta: Find a word meaning ‘someone unfairly blamed for a problem’.
preguntas.cita: its critics are not merely populists in search of a scapegoat
preguntas.explicacion: A “scapegoat” (es: chivo expiatorio) is the person or institution unfairly blamed for problems.

preguntas.pregunta: Why, according to the author, is the legitimacy of central banks now being questioned?
opciones: Because they refused to buy government bonds after 2008
Because their expanded powers have large distributional consequences
Because they have abandoned inflation targets
Because their governors are elected by parliament
respuestas: Because their expanded powers have large distributional consequences
preguntas.cita: Decisions with such large distributional consequences inevitably invite the question: who gave them the right?
preguntas.explicacion: After 2008 central banks took on much greater powers (bond purchases, supervision, bailouts) with redistributive effects, which raises the question of their legitimacy. They did buy bonds, and the text does not say that they abandoned their targets.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: Most central banks reacted immediately to the inflation surge of 2021–23.
preguntas.cita: Most central banks were slow to react, initially describing the rise in prices as transitory.
preguntas.explicacion: The text states the opposite: they reacted late because at first they considered the rise in prices to be transitory.

preguntas.enunciado: Find a word in paragraph 4 that means “a formal accusation, a set of charges”.
preguntas.pregunta: Find a word meaning ‘a formal accusation or list of charges’.
preguntas.cita: added a further charge to the indictment
preguntas.explicacion: An “indictment” is the formal charge in criminal proceedings; here it is used figuratively for the list of criticisms against central banks. It is pronounced /ɪnˈdaɪt-/, without the c.

preguntas.pregunta: How does political pressure on central banks usually manifest itself, according to the article?
opciones: Through the outright abolition of their independence
Through a series of subtle steps that gradually erode their credibility
Through strikes by central bank staff
respuestas: Through a series of subtle steps that gradually erode their credibility
preguntas.cita: Pressure on central banks rarely takes the form of an outright abolition of their independence. It is subtler
preguntas.explicacion: The author explains that pressure is rarely an open abolition; it consists of subtle steps (attacks, appointments of like-minded people, threats) which, together, erode credibility.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: The author names Argentina and Turkey as recent examples of runaway inflation.
preguntas.explicacion: The text speaks of “countries” that forced their central banks to keep interest rates low, but it does not name any.

preguntas.enunciado: Find a word in paragraph 7 that means “the obligation to explain and justify one's actions”.
preguntas.pregunta: Find a word meaning ‘the obligation to explain and justify one’s decisions’.
preguntas.cita: Independence is defensible only if it comes with accountability.
preguntas.explicacion: “Accountability” (es: rendición de cuentas) is the obligation to answer to those who grant power, here to parliament and citizens.

preguntas.pregunta: How should the interdependence between central banks and public budgets be managed?
opciones: Through informal talks between the governor and the finance minister
Through clear rules on bond purchases and on sharing profits and losses
By banning central banks from holding public debt
By merging the central bank with the treasury
respuestas: Through clear rules on bond purchases and on sharing profits and losses
preguntas.cita: it should be managed through clear rules on bond purchases and on how losses or profits are shared with the treasury
preguntas.explicacion: The author calls for clear rules instead of informal pressure “behind closed doors”. He does not propose banning holdings of debt or merging institutions.

preguntas.enunciado: Answer in your own words (1–3 sentences).
preguntas.pregunta: What is ‘the paradox of independence’ described in the final paragraph?
respuestas: Central bank independence is meant to protect monetary policy from politics, yet it ultimately depends on politics, because laws and treaties can be changed. It survives only as long as there is a broad political consensus in favour of price stability.
preguntas.cita: The paradox of independence is that it depends on politics.
preguntas.explicacion: The paradox is that an institution created to stand apart from politics only exists as long as politics supports it through a broad consensus.

tribunal.pregunta: What is the main argument of the article?
tribunal.pista_es: Comprehension: the author's thesis and its condition (accountability).
ideas: Independence should be defended
It protects against the short-term inflation bias of governments
It must be accompanied by accountability

tribunal.pista_es: Explain the political business cycle and the inflation bias.
ideas: Electoral cycle and short-term benefits
Lower debt-service costs

tribunal.pista_es: Opinion on the expansion of the mandate (asset purchases, supervision, climate).
ideas: Quantitative easing was necessary in a crisis

tribunal.pregunta: How is the independence of the European Central Bank guaranteed, and how is it held accountable?
tribunal.pista_es: EU institutional framework: the Treaty, the ban on monetary financing, the European Parliament.
ideas: Independence enshrined in the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU
Prohibition of monetary financing of governments
Primary mandate of price stability

tribunal.pista_es: Link to Spain: integration into the Eurosystem and current functions.
ideas: Part of the Eurosystem; no longer sets interest rates alone
Banking supervision within the Single Supervisory Mechanism
Economic analysis and advice
Independence under Spanish law since the 1990s

tribunal.pista_es: Fiscal dominance and the risk of fragmentation in the euro area.
ideas: Fiscal dominance risk
Rate rises increase interest bills
Instruments against fragmentation and their conditions
Need for credible fiscal rules

tribunal.pista_es: Opinion: single mandate versus dual or broader mandate.
ideas: The US Federal Reserve has a dual mandate
Wider mandates may dilute focus and legitimacy
Climate risks affect financial stability
